newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Africa summit ends, backing Sierra Leone democracy.
newsitem.headline: Africa summit ends, backing Sierra Leone democracy.

text.p: African leaders ended their annual stocktaking on Wednesday with a ringing endorsement of efforts to restore democracy in Sierra Leone and hints that Nigeria and Burundi could be next to come under peer pressure to reform.

The Organisation of African Unity's new chairman, Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe, and Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim told a news conference after a three-day OAU summit the continent was done with military rule, dictatorship and coups.
Echoing the theme of many speeches to the summit calling for democracy throughout Africa, they said the OAU would seek to persuade members to pursue democracy and to shun force.
"We are getting tougher and tougher each time. I can assure you that for future coups it will be much tougher," Mugabe said.
"We want to (ensure) that conflict is avoided, democracy is not reversed and, where it is reversed, that we attend to the situation as we are trying to do in Sierra Leone and Burundi."

The two men threw the full weight of the 53-nation OAU behind the Nigerian-led military mission to reverse the May 25 military takeover in Sierra Leone and restore civilian President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah to power.
"We unanimously and unreservedly condemned the coup d'etat in Sierra Leone as an enormous setback for democracy in Africa," Mugabe said in a closing address to the summit.

Leaders at the summit repeatedly welcomed Laurent Kabila's takeover in the former Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo, but the backing came with an insistence that he implement his promise to hold elections within two years.

"We are going to help them in their programme for rehabilitation and reconstruction and also to help them and encourage them in their commitment towards democratisation, towards better respect for human rights," Salim said.
Salim and Mugabe said OAU envoys had already made it clear to Nigerian ruler Sani Abacha and President Pierre Buyoya of Burundi that their military regimes were unacceptable.
"Ten or so years ago we did not address, as the OAU, issues that had to do with coups d'etat as such. We merely regretted that they had occurred," Mugabe said.
"But now we want to address them and address them as vigorously as we can," he said.

The summit endorsed the OAU's existing call for the lifting of sanctions against Libya following the 1988 Lockerbie airline bombing and renewed its support for Palestinians in their struggle for land with Israel.
"We are saying that Libya should be allowed to develop its economy without sanctions. The people of Libya have suffered enough," Mugabe told the news conference.
The summit resolved to press Africa's demand for at least two permanent seats on an expanded 26-member U.N. Security Council and called for the abolition of existing veto rights.
Delegates resolved to pursue a 50-year programme to achieve an African common market by 2030, calling on member states to enact laws to relax trade barriers and promote regional integration.
Organisers said the next summit would be in Burkina Faso in the first week of June 1998.
